title: Therapy Isn't Working: What to Do When You're Stuck
description: Signs therapy isn't helping, reasons why, and what to do next. When to switch therapists, try a different approach, or add medication.

content.text: You've been going to therapy but nothing's changing. Is it you? The therapist? The approach? Here's how to figure out what's wrong and what to do.
Signs Therapy Isn't Working

items: Therapist seems checked out or distracted
You're not using anything from therapy in real life

content.text: Why Therapy Might Not Be Working
Wrong Approach

Not all therapy is the same. If you have OCD and you're doing insight-oriented talk therapy, it won't help—you need ERP. If you have trauma and you're doing general CBT, you might need EMDR or prolonged exposure.
Poor Fit with Therapist
The relationship matters more than the technique. If you don't feel understood, safe, or connected, the therapy won't work regardless of approach.
Not Doing the Work
Therapy requires active participation. If you're not doing homework, practicing skills, or being honest in sessions, progress will stall.
Need Medication
Sometimes symptoms are too severe for therapy to work alone. Medication can create enough relief to engage in therapy effectively.
Wrong Diagnosis
If the underlying problem is misidentified (e.g., treating anxiety when it's ADHD), the treatment won't match.
What to Do
Talk to Your Therapist
Before anything else, bring it up. 'I'm not sure therapy is helping. Can we talk about what's working and what isn't?' A good therapist will welcome this conversation.
Get Specific About What's Not Working

items: Do you not feel comfortable with the therapist?
Are you not applying what you learn?

content.text: Consider Changes

items: Different approach (ask about CBT, EMDR, DBT, etc.)
Different therapist (it's okay, they won't take it personally)
More intensive treatment (IOP, PHP) if needed

content.text: Therapy involves temporary discomfort—processing difficult emotions isn't fun. The question is whether you're making progress despite the discomfort, or just suffering without moving forward.
The Bottom Line

Therapy should help. If it's not, something needs to change—the approach, the therapist, or what you're doing in and out of sessions. Don't stay stuck for months hoping it'll click. Name the problem and make adjustments.
